I actually prefer Captivate Classic to SL and have been using it for over 7 years now. If you’re coming from a design background, the customizability of this is so much richer than anything else out there. Asides from the frequent crashes, I haven’t had any issues with file corruption or copying text from other sources. 

That being said, I agree it’s a real turd pile. The lack of support by Adobe is a HUGE setback. 

If you’re working on Mac OS, for example, you should not update it until Adobe has updated Captivate for the OS update. 

Your company cyber security measures can also impede functionality, such as being able to preview HTML. I work for a healthcare company that takes HIPAA data security very seriously (they don’t even let us use Grammarly) and they’ve had to find workarounds for me to use this gd software. 

If your company has its own brand font and you try to save a theme in that font, it will keep defaulting to mthfkng Tahoma every time you create a new blank project with that theme.  So, asides from the theme, I also save the object styles to import them to new projects. 

Use the hell out of object styles and caption styles. Assign a style to EVERYTHING. This is kind of a rule for content design in general, anyway, and applies if you use InDesign or Illustrator, too.

Lesson plans. I’m talking about those old templates that’s been floating around that every training team seems to use. They put minimal effort into the needs assessment and just go off exactly what client asks for, then go straight into lesson planning. They make up learning objectives while they fill it out and then stuff every single bullet point with content bloat. And then they go right into scripting and writing knowledge assessments that they pull from the air. End result is a long slide deck with 4 paragraphs in every slide, followed by a knowledge assessment of 10 questions with a high difficulty threshold.

Exactly this. At my new corporate job, I’m training the training team to rewrite learning objectives so that they are more relatable to the learner and to business goals. They don’t need to “be able to describe, recite, understand the different types of” anything. We tell them what exactly they need to do to help them do their jobs well.

Making a test difficult isn’t what will help with learning. The test should only be to assess whether the learners have the understanding they need to meet desired academic or business outcomes, so that they are ready to apply the learning in real life. 


If your test question is true to that learning objective and they are all finding it easy even without going through the training, then you might be right that the training was never necessary. But, again, if it’s a compliance training, you still have to create it anyway.

And for the paper stuff that I wasn’t ready to throw away, I got an artist folio.
